modules.title: Ruby Language Basics
modules.intro: Ruby interview questions for freshers and beginners start with the language fundamentals every interviewer expects you to know. This module covers data types (Integer, Float, String, Symbol, Array, Hash, NilClass, TrueClass, FalseClass), variables (local, instance, class, global, constants), string interpolation with double-quoted strings, nil and Ruby's truthiness rules (only nil and false are falsy — 0 and empty string are truthy), the Symbol vs String distinction at a basic level, Array and Hash operations that come up in every interview, conditionals and loops (if, unless, case/when, each, times, while), and defining methods with default arguments. Every answer uses beginner-level language — no internals, no GVL, no object allocation. Just the Ruby a junior developer needs to know on day one.

modules.title: Ruby OOP Basics
modules.intro: Ruby OOP basics interview questions cover the object-oriented concepts every junior Ruby developer needs to explain confidently. This module covers class definition and instantiation, the initialize method and constructor arguments, instance variables (@name) and instance methods, attr_accessor/attr_reader/attr_writer and what each generates (no magic — they define getter and setter methods), class methods with self., inheritance with < and calling super, the four OOP pillars in Ruby (encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism) with concrete Ruby examples, public/private/protected method visibility, self in different contexts, and duck typing — why respond_to? is more Ruby than is_a?. Every answer includes a minimal runnable Ruby example.

modules.title: Blocks & Iterators
modules.intro: Blocks and iterators are uniquely Ruby and come up in virtually every Ruby fresher interview. This module covers block syntax (do...end for multi-line, curly braces for one-liners), how yield calls the block from inside a method, block_given? to check if a block was passed, and the core Enumerable methods every Ruby developer must know: each (iterate, returns original array), map/collect (transform, returns new array), select/filter (keep matching elements), reject (remove matching elements), find/detect (first match), reduce/inject (accumulate), any?, all?, none?, count, sort, sort_by, each_with_index, and each_with_object. Also covers the symbol-to-proc shorthand &:method_name and method chaining. The most common interview mistake: confusing each (returns original) with map (returns new array).

modules.title: Error Handling Basics
modules.intro: Ruby exception handling interview questions test whether you understand how errors propagate and how to handle them safely. This module covers the begin/rescue/ensure/end structure, raise with a message string vs raising a specific exception class, how to capture the exception object with rescue ErrorClass => e, the standard exception hierarchy (Exception → StandardError → RuntimeError — rescue catches StandardError and below by default, so never rescue Exception), ensure always runs (like finally in other languages), retry inside a rescue block with a counter to prevent infinite loops, defining custom exception classes with class PaymentError < StandardError; end, and the rescue statement modifier for simple one-liners. Every answer explains the why — what happens at runtime, not just the syntax.

modules.title: Ruby Modules Basics
modules.intro: Ruby modules interview questions cover two key uses: namespacing and mixins. This module covers the module as namespace (module Animals; class Dog; end; end → Animals::Dog), include for adding instance methods to a class, extend for adding module methods as class-level methods, the basic include vs extend difference, Enumerable — what you get for implementing each (map, select, sort, min, max, group_by, and more), Comparable — what you get for implementing <=> (all comparison operators and between? and clamp), why Ruby uses modules for mixins instead of multiple inheritance, and the ancestors chain as the simple mental model for method lookup. Examples stay at beginner level — no prepend, no MRO tracing.

modules.title: Rails Basics
modules.intro: Rails basics interview questions for freshers cover what interviewers expect a junior Rails developer to know walking in. This module covers Rails MVC (Model — data and business logic, View — presentation, Controller — orchestration and glue), convention over configuration and what it means in practice, the directory structure of a new Rails app and what lives where, routes (resources :posts generates 7 RESTful routes — know all 7), controller basics (inherits from ApplicationController, actions are public methods, params hash), the difference between render (same request, same action) and redirect_to (new HTTP request), instance variables in controllers that flow to views, before_action, flash messages, and the most useful Rails console commands. Every answer traces the full request → response path.

modules.title: Rails Forms & Views
modules.intro: Rails views and forms interview questions test whether you understand the presentation layer that delivers HTML to the browser. This module covers ERB syntax (<%=  %> outputs and escapes, <% %> executes without output, <%# %> is a comment), layouts and the yield keyword for content injection, partials with render and the locals option for passing data, form_with and how it generates CSRF tokens automatically, the common view helpers (link_to, button_to, image_tag, number_to_currency, pluralize, humanize), content_for and yield with a named block for page-specific content, flash display in layouts, iterating with .each in ERB templates, and why automatic HTML escaping in ERB protects against XSS. All examples are beginner-level — no decorators, no ViewComponent.

modules.title: Active Record Basics
modules.intro: Active Record basics interview questions for freshers cover the database layer that every Rails developer touches every day. This module covers the ORM concept (the model maps to a database table — Post model → posts table, user_id foreign key), CRUD operations (create/find/find_by/all/where/update/save/destroy) and the bang vs non-bang semantics (save returns boolean, save! raises exception), validations (presence, uniqueness, format) and how to check valid? and read errors.full_messages, basic associations (belongs_to adds the foreign key, has_many is the inverse), dependent: :destroy for cascade deletion, migrations (rails generate model, the change method, db:migrate, db:rollback), schema.rb as the source of truth, and scopes at a basic level. Every answer shows the Ruby code and explains the SQL it produces.

modules.title: Rails API Basics
modules.intro: Rails API interview questions for freshers should connect HTTP contracts to the Rails request stack. This module explains full versus API-only applications, truthful method and status-code choices, stable JSON representations, the complete Rack-to-controller request cycle, and resourceful Rails routes. Each lesson distinguishes framework convenience from protocol responsibility and uses a valid controller or routing example.

modules.title: OOP & Design Basics
modules.intro: Object-oriented design basics interview questions test whether you can think about code structure, not just write code that works. This module covers the four OOP pillars with Ruby examples (encapsulation — private methods and instance variables, abstraction — expose a clean interface, inheritance — class Dog < Animal, polymorphism — same method name different behavior), the BankAccount class design exercise interviewers use to test OOP thinking, DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) — recognising duplication and extracting a method, Keep It Simple, the Ruby naming conventions interviewers care about (predicate methods end with ?, mutating methods end with !, constants in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE), and SOLID at a concept level (single responsibility — one class, one job; open/closed — open to extension). All explanations stay at fresher depth — no service objects, no hexagonal architecture.

modules.title: Rails Testing Basics
modules.intro: Rails testing basics interview questions for freshers cover enough testing knowledge to pass a junior-level interview. This module covers why tests matter (regression safety, refactoring confidence, living documentation), the test pyramid at a basic level (unit vs integration vs end-to-end), RSpec syntax (describe, context, it, expect(x).to eq(y)), Minitest assertions (assert_equal, assert_nil, assert_raises, refute), how to run tests (rails test vs bundle exec rspec), model tests that verify validations and basic methods, controller tests that verify response status and redirects, fixtures vs FactoryBot (test data helpers), the test database (separate DB that resets between runs), and the red-green-refactor cycle. Every answer includes a minimal test example.

modules.title: Git & Bundler Basics
modules.intro: Git and Bundler interview questions for Ruby freshers cover the daily workflow tools every developer needs to use from day one. This module covers the git commands every developer runs daily (init, clone, status, add, commit, push, pull), branches and the feature branch workflow, pull requests and what a code review process looks like, .gitignore and what to exclude (.env, tmp/, log/, coverage/), merge conflict basics (how to identify and resolve), Bundler (bundle install, bundle exec, bundle update), the Gemfile (specifying gems with version constraints), the Gemfile.lock (locks exact versions — commit it so every developer runs the same gems), the difference between gem install and bundler in a project context, semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH and what ~> 2.5 means), and the .ruby-version file.

modules.title: Behavioral & Fresher Q&A
modules.intro: Behavioral interview questions for Ruby freshers require answers that are honest, specific, and show genuine interest in the craft. This module covers the 60-second self-introduction for a junior Ruby developer (structure: who I am, what I've built, why Ruby, what I'm looking for), talking about college or bootcamp projects using the STAR format (Situation, Task, Action, Result — keep it under 2 minutes), answering why Ruby on Rails with an authentic response, the weakness question framed as an area of active growth with steps you are actually taking, handling questions you don't know the answer to (show curiosity — explain what you would do to find out), questions to ask the interviewer that signal genuine interest, how to stay current with Ruby and Rails (RubyWeekly, the Rails blog, reading gem source code), and the most common fresher interview mistakes to avoid.

modules.title: DSA Basics in Ruby
modules.intro: DSA and coding-round questions appear even in Ruby fresher interviews — especially at companies that use HackerRank or CoderPad. Ruby's expressive built-ins (Enumerable, Array methods, Hash) make many problems elegant, but you still need to know the patterns. This module covers the most common fresher coding patterns: array/hash manipulation with Ruby idioms, string methods and freeze, the two-pointer technique, when to use .sort vs .sort_by, Big-O reasoning (why does .include? on an Array differ from a Set?), and the five coding patterns that recur most often in Ruby screening rounds.

modules.title: SQL & Database Basics for Rails Developers
modules.intro: SQL and database basics are tested in every Rails fresher interview. Even if you only ever write ActiveRecord, interviewers expect you to understand what SQL it generates, why it generates that SQL, and how to spot and fix an N+1 query. This module covers the SQL that every fresher must know (SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, the four JOIN types), how ActiveRecord maps to SQL, designing a simple schema with foreign keys, writing and running a migration, and the N+1 pattern with its .includes fix — the single most commonly asked Rails interview question at the fresher level.

modules.title: Sidekiq & Background Jobs Intro
modules.intro: Sidekiq and background-job questions test whether a Rails developer understands the complete asynchronous lifecycle, not only `perform_async`. This module covers when work belongs outside a request, how web and worker processes share a queue store, native Sidekiq payloads and idempotency, retry and dead-job handling, and the Active Job adapter boundary. Each lesson distinguishes successful enqueueing from completed business work and treats failure, duplicate execution, monitoring, and deployment compatibility as part of the feature.

modules.title: Modern Ruby (3.x) Features
modules.intro: Modern Ruby interview questions should test whether a developer understands the contracts behind newer syntax, not whether they can list release notes. This module teaches structural pattern matching, concise block parameters, endless method definitions, Data value objects, and frozen string literals through small examples and explicit boundaries. Each lesson explains what the feature changes, what remains ordinary Ruby behaviour, where the shorthand improves clarity, and where a conventional class, method, block, or mutable string is safer.

modules.title: Ruby Debugging & Developer Tools
modules.intro: Ruby debugging questions test whether a developer can turn a failure into evidence and a durable fix. This module covers execution control with Byebug and Pry, the current Rails debugger context, common runtime exception contracts, safe Rails console investigation, ordered backtrace reading, and team use of RuboCop. Every lesson begins with the failed assumption, uses a concrete example, distinguishes observation from mutation, and ends with a reproducible test or review boundary rather than a temporary debugging trick.

modules.title: Rails Authentication Basics
modules.intro: Rails authentication questions test whether a junior developer can explain identity across requests without confusing the available mechanisms. This module traces Devise through Warden and Rails sessions, separates plain, signed, encrypted, and session cookies, and compares opaque and signed bearer tokens without claiming token authentication is automatically stateless. Security boundaries—authorization, CSRF, token storage, expiry, and revocation—remain explicit in every answer.

modules.title: Ruby File I/O & Serialization
modules.intro: Ruby I/O and serialization questions test safe resource handling at real system boundaries. This focused module covers whole-file helpers versus streaming, File.open block cleanup, access modes and atomic replacement, plus interoperable JSON and safe YAML parsing. Array, Hash, and Enumerable material remains in the canonical language and iterator modules instead of being duplicated here.

modules.title: Ruby & Rails Security Basics
modules.intro: Rails security basics should teach where data crosses into a trusted interpreter or model boundary. This module covers SQL value binding and dynamic-identifier allowlists, Strong Parameters as mass-assignment shape filtering rather than authorization, and context-aware XSS prevention through escaping, sanitization, safe browser sinks, and defense in depth. Each lesson corrects a common oversimplification and includes a concrete Rails example.
